steps.title: Reading comprehension — the working method
steps.intro: 6–7 minutes per passage, reading included: read only what the questions need.

tables.title: Question types
head: Type
How to spot it
What to read
rows: From one sentence before; several lines → just those
No place given, no "according to the text"
Between the question before and after
"according to the text" (the last question may omit it)
Skip, mark, solve last — use what you gathered

tables.title: Steps
head: Do this
rows: Read the question — without the choices
Read the part of the passage it points to
Read the question with the choices, and answer
Repeat for every specific question, in order

tips: Answer only from the passage, never from general knowledge.
Questions follow the passage order — general questions can appear anywhere.
A name you never met in the passage is probably invented for the question — don't hunt for it.
Short on time: read the first sentence of each paragraph (or first + last).

steps.stem: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the sentence "The pattern, however, is a tendency rather than a law … the pattern predicts" (paragraph 1)?
choices: Not every island species conforms to the pattern: many have not changed in size at all, and some have even changed in the opposite direction
Most island species conform to the pattern, and those that do not conform to it have changed in size in the opposite direction
Since many island species have not changed in size, the direction of change that the pattern predicts is often the wrong one
A few island species have changed in size in the predicted direction, but a great many have not changed in size at all
explanation: The sentence names two exceptions: many species that did not change and a few that changed the other way. (2) adds "most" and merges the two groups, (3) turns "no change" into evidence of the wrong direction, and (4) attaches "a few" to the species that follow the pattern.

steps.stem: Why do large animals tend to become smaller on islands, according to the most widely accepted explanation (paragraph 2)?
choices: Because the area of an island is too small to hold animals of a large size
Because on an island, smaller animals find it easier to hide from predators
Because when food runs short, the individuals that need less food are more likely to survive and leave offspring
Because the food that grows on islands is of poorer quality than the food on the mainland, and a large body cannot be sustained by it
explanation: The paragraph links size to the amount of food: a smaller body gets through a lean season, and over generations the population shrinks. (1) is what the refinement of this explanation denies, (2) belongs to the other explanation (paragraph 3), and (4) speaks of quality, which the paragraph never mentions.

steps.stem: Two populations of the same species of wild goat live on two islands of equal area. The goats on the first island are considerably smaller than those on the second. According to the refinement that some researchers proposed to the explanation from food, which of the following could explain this?
choices: The first island is farther from the mainland than the second
The first island provides less food for each goat than the second
There are more predators on the first island than on the second
The second island consists mostly of bare rock, whereas the first is covered with dense vegetation
explanation: According to the refinement of the explanation from food, the food available to each animal, not the island's area, decides how strongly small bodies are favored. (4) reverses the two islands, and (1) and (3) name factors the hypothesis does not use; more predators would, if anything, favor larger bodies.

steps.stem: Which of the following is not correct regarding the explanation from predators (paragraph 3)?
choices: It holds that the absence of predators can account both for the growth of small animals and for the shrinking of large ones
It assumes that a very large body can protect a grazing animal from predators
It predicts that species living on islands without predators will change in size
It is more convincing for the shrinking of large animals than for the growth of small ones
explanation: The paragraph says this of the explanation from food, and presents the predator explanation's merit as covering both directions. (1), (2) and (3) are each stated in the paragraph.

steps.stem: Which of the following findings in the study described in paragraph 4 would have supported the explanation from predators?
choices: Lizards on the snake-free islands differ in size from lizards on islands with snakes that have a similar supply of insects
The size of the lizards on each island corresponds closely to the number of insects on which they feed on that island
The snakes reached the islands only a relatively short time ago
The lizards are of the same size on all of the islands in the chain
explanation: The researchers said the predator explanation required a size difference between snake-free and snake islands even where food was similar. (2) is the actual finding, which supports the food explanation; (3) is the researchers' caution, which may excuse the predator explanation but does not support it; (4) supports neither explanation.

steps.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the text?
choices: Animals on islands always change in size, in whichever direction the local supply of food dictates
The size of an animal is not fixed, but is a compromise among pressures that the conditions on an island can change
The explanation from food has been shown to be correct, and the explanation from predators has been refuted
Island animals are smaller than their mainland relatives because islands offer less food and fewer predators
explanation: The last paragraph draws the general lesson that the whole passage builds toward. (1) says "always," which paragraph 1 denies; (3) overstates a study whose conclusion is limited to "these islands, at least"; (4) ignores the small animals that grow larger.

steps.stem: Which of the following is not mentioned in the first paragraph as a reason that the documents of the Cairo Geniza were preserved?
choices: the custom of not destroying writings that contain the name of God
the dry climate of Egypt, in which paper and parchment decay slowly
the fact that the room was not emptied, as was customary, for hundreds of years
the fact that the community kept a list of the documents placed in the room
explanation: The paragraph mentions the custom, the unemptied room and the dry climate; a list of the documents is not mentioned.

steps.stem: The fragment that the Lewis and Gibson sisters showed Schechter was important because -
choices: it was the oldest document that had been found in the geniza
it was part of a work whose original language had been known until then mainly through a translation
it proved that the geniza was located in the Ben Ezra Synagogue
it was the first fragment from the geniza that had reached a European scholar, and it led Schechter to travel to Cairo
explanation: Ben Sira had been known mainly from its Greek translation. (4) contradicts the first sentence of the second paragraph, and (1) and (3) are not stated.

steps.stem: According to the third paragraph, which of the following statements about the fragments that Schechter sent to Cambridge is correct?
choices: They are only part of the contents of the geniza, the rest of which is kept today in libraries in several countries
They include all the documents that were in the geniza when Schechter arrived in Cairo
They were bought from dealers in Cairo with money that Taylor and the Chief Rabbi of Britain had given Schechter for this purpose
They were sorted by Schechter into literary and documentary texts before he left Cairo
explanation: Schechter removed "a very large part" of the contents, and other parts are in dozens of libraries. (2) contradicts "a very large part," (3) confuses the letter of recommendation with money and the community's consent with a purchase, and (4) is not mentioned.

steps.stem: According to the fourth paragraph, why did the documentary material of the geniza receive little attention at first?
choices: because it made up only a small part of the collection
because it reached the libraries only after the literary texts had been studied
because the first researchers were looking mainly for literary and religious works
because it was written in Judeo-Arabic, which the first researchers did not consider part of Jewish literature
explanation: The paragraph contrasts what the first researchers searched for with the documents they neglected. (1) contradicts "a considerable part," and (2) and (4) give reasons the text does not give; the language is mentioned only as a fact about the documents.

steps.stem: According to the way Goitein used the geniza documents, it is likely that a list of the household goods of a family from the twelfth century found in the geniza -
choices: would be of little value to a historian, since it does not contain a literary or religious text
could provide information about the daily life of the family that owned the goods
would be useful only if the name of the person who wrote it were known
would be important mainly as evidence of the Hebrew language of the period
explanation: Goitein used such documents to describe daily life, including clothes and food. (1) is the attitude of the first researchers, (4) ignores that most such documents are in Judeo-Arabic, and (3) is not implied.

steps.stem: Which of the following is not implied in the last paragraph?
choices: Parts of one document may be kept in different libraries
Computer programs can help to identify fragments that belong to the same document
Most of the fragments of the geniza have already been joined to the other parts of the documents to which they belong
Before the fragments were photographed, joining them often required comparing originals that were kept in different places
explanation: The paragraph says computers help to locate parts; it does not say that most fragments have been joined. (1), (2) and (4) are stated or implied.

steps.stem: Which of the following questions is not answered in the first paragraph?
choices: How much rain falls on average each year in the Negev highlands?
When was the Nabatean kingdom annexed to the Roman Empire?
How many people lived in Avdat when it was at its peak?
Why is it surprising that fields existed in the area?
explanation: The paragraph gives the rainfall, the year 106 CE and the reason for surprise, but not the population of Avdat.

steps.stem: "this ratio" (paragraph 2) is the ratio between -
choices: the area from which the runoff was collected and the area of the field that received it
the amount of rain that falls on the slopes and the amount that sinks into them
the length of the walls in the wadi and the width of the wadi
the amount of water that reached a field and the amount of crops that were grown in it each year
explanation: Each field received the rain of an area many times larger; the ratio is between these areas. (2) confuses the ratio with the crust effect, and (3) and (4) are not discussed.

steps.stem: Which of the following best reflects the process described in the second paragraph by which the rain reached the fields?
choices: rain falls on the slopes → the water sinks into the loess → the soil of the slopes becomes moist → the moisture passes underground to the fields in the wadi
rain falls in the wadi → the terrace walls stop the water → the water rises up the slopes → a crust forms on the soil of the fields
rain falls on the slopes → the water is collected in cisterns dug in the rock → it is carried to the fields in jars → it is poured behind the terrace walls
rain falls on the slopes → a thin crust forms on the loess → the water flows down into the channels → it is held behind the walls of the terraces
explanation: The crust makes the water flow down, the channels collect it, and the walls hold it. (1) contradicts the crust, which prevents the water from sinking in; (2) reverses the direction of the flow; (3) describes a method the text does not mention.

steps.stem: According to the third paragraph, the experiment carried out near Avdat -
choices: proved that the ancient farms had been built by the Nabateans
showed that crops could be grown in the area using runoff alone
showed that the ancient farms had required more rain than falls near Avdat today
showed that fruit trees could not be grown in the area without additional water
explanation: Crops grew without any water other than runoff. (1) is contradicted by the last paragraph, and (3) and (4) contradict the results.

steps.stem: Which of the following findings would be most consistent with Evenari's explanation of the stone heaps (paragraph 4)?
choices: Remains of the roots of grapevines are found inside many of the heaps, at a depth of several centimeters
The heaps are found mainly in the beds of the wadis, close to the fields that received the runoff
The heaps were built in the modern period by shepherds, who used them to mark the boundaries of grazing areas
During rain, more water flows down slopes cleared of stones than down similar slopes that were not cleared
explanation: Evenari's explanation rests on the claim that cleared slopes produce more runoff. (1) supports the older explanation, (2) contradicts the location of the heaps on the slopes, and (3) contradicts his view that the farmers made them.

steps.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the last paragraph?
choices: The common name of the fields may be misleading as to the period in which many of them were built
The Nabateans did not practice agriculture in the Negev
The fields were abandoned when the Nabatean kingdom was annexed to the Roman Empire in 106 CE
Evenari was the first to show that the fields dated from the Byzantine period
explanation: They are called Nabatean, but many were built in the Byzantine period. (2) goes beyond "many of them," (3) contradicts the paragraph, and (4) attributes the dating to Evenari, whereas the text speaks of later research.

steps.stem: According to the first paragraph, the boat was discovered because -
choices: a drought had lowered the level of the lake and exposed parts of its shore
the antiquities authorities had begun a survey of the shore of the lake
a storm had washed away the mud that covered the boat
the kibbutz had begun to build a new pier on the shore
explanation: The drought exposed the shore, where the brothers noticed the boat. (2) reverses the order (the authorities were informed afterwards), and (3) and (4) are not mentioned.

steps.stem: Why did the team have to work "day and night" (paragraph 2)?
choices: because the outline of the boat could be seen only when the lake was calm
because the wood would dry out and crack if the work continued for more than a few days
because the polyurethane foam had to be applied before the wood hardened
because the level of the lake was expected to rise and cover the site
explanation: The rains had begun and the lake was expected to rise. (2) confuses the reason for the haste with the reason for keeping the wood wet, which was done throughout the work; (1) and (3) are not stated.

steps.stem: The fact that about twelve types of wood were identified in the boat (paragraph 3) is presented as evidence that -
choices: the boat was built by several builders at the same time
the boat was built outside the Galilee and brought to the lake
the boat had been repaired many times, partly with parts of other boats
good wood was plentiful in the Galilee at that time
explanation: The paragraph draws this conclusion from the variety of the wood. (4) contradicts "some of them of poor quality," and (1) and (2) are not stated.

steps.stem: Which of the following statements about the dating of the boat is correct according to the fourth paragraph?
choices: The carbon-14 test dated the boat more precisely than the objects found near it, and therefore the objects were not taken into account
The objects found near the boat and the carbon-14 test of its wood point to approximately the same period
The dating was based on the method of construction alone, since no objects were found near the boat
The carbon-14 test showed that the boat was built later than the objects found near it were made
explanation: The results of the carbon-14 test pointed to approximately the same period as the pot and the lamp. (3) contradicts the finding of the objects, and (1) and (4) are not stated.

steps.stem: Which of the following is not mentioned in the text as a step taken in order to preserve the boat?
choices: keeping the wood wet throughout the excavation, which lasted eleven days
covering the boat with polyurethane foam
replacing the water in the wood with a synthetic wax
drying the wood slowly in a room in which the humidity was controlled
explanation: The text mentions the other three steps; slow drying in a controlled room is not mentioned.

steps.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the text?
choices: An Ancient Boat from the Sea of Galilee: Discovery, Excavation, Dating and Conservation
Fishing on the Sea of Galilee in the First Century
The Effect of the Droughts of the 1980s on the Level of the Sea of Galilee and on Its Shores
Methods of Dating Ancient Wooden Objects
explanation: The text follows the boat from its discovery to its display. (2), (3) and (4) each take one detail.

steps.stem: According to the first paragraph, which of the following is correct?
choices: The level of the Dead Sea has been falling by about one meter every year since the 1930s
The level of the Dead Sea fell by about forty meters between the 1930s and the 1960s
The rate at which the level of the Dead Sea falls has increased over the years
In the 1930s, the surface of the Dead Sea was about 430 meters below sea level
explanation: The level fell by tens of centimeters a year at first and by about a meter a year from the 1990s. (1) ignores the change in rate, (2) places the decline before it began, and (4) confuses the 1930s with 2016.

steps.stem: Which of the following is not presented in the second paragraph as a cause of the decline in the level of the Dead Sea?
choices: the diversion of water from the Jordan River and its tributaries by three countries
an increase in the rate of evaporation from the surface of the lake
the pumping of water from the northern basin into evaporation ponds
the construction of dams on the tributaries of the Yarmouk River
explanation: The paragraph says the evaporation has not decreased, not that it has increased. (1), (3) and (4) are presented as causes.

steps.stem: According to the third paragraph, the rise in the water level in the southern ponds results from -
choices: the flow of water from the northern basin through a natural channel
the rain that falls in the area in winter
the pumping of larger amounts of water into the ponds every year
the layer of salt that accumulates on the floor of the ponds
explanation: The salt layer grows every year and raises the water. (3) invents a change in the pumping, and (1) and (2) are not stated.

steps.stem: Which of the following best reflects the process described in the fourth paragraph?
choices: the level of the lake falls → salty water flows into the buried salt layer → the salt layer grows thicker → the ground above it rises and cracks
the level of the lake falls → fresh groundwater reaches the buried salt layer → the salt dissolves and cavities form → the soil above a cavity collapses
the level of the lake falls → the mud of the exposed shore dries → deep cracks form in it → the ground collapses into the cracks
the level of the lake falls → salty groundwater rises to the surface → the salt crystallizes on the shore → holes form in the salt crust
explanation: The paragraph describes fresh water reaching the salt layer and dissolving it. (1) reverses the role of the salty water, and (3) and (4) describe processes the text does not mention.

steps.stem: The story of Eli Raz (paragraph 5) is mentioned in order to -
choices: illustrate that the sinkholes endanger not only property but also people
show that the geologists in the area did not know about the sinkholes until the early 2000s
explain how the first sinkholes were discovered
show that sinkholes form only in places that people rarely visit
explanation: The story follows "The danger is not only to property." (2) and (3) contradict the fact that the first sinkholes were noticed in the 1980s and that Raz had been documenting them for years, and (4) is not stated.

steps.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the text?
choices: The sinkholes were caused mainly by the evaporation ponds in the southern part of the lake
The hotels at Ein Bokek are threatened mainly by sinkholes
Stopping the decline in the level of the lake would probably slow the formation of new sinkholes
Since the 1970s, the water level in the southern ponds has fallen by about one meter a year
explanation: The sinkholes form because the falling level lets fresh water reach the salt. (2) confuses the threat of rising water with sinkholes, (4) confuses the south with the north, and (1) is not stated.

steps.stem: The mention that Körnicke examined the specimen "eighteen years later" (paragraph 2) shows -
choices: that Kotschy did not know on which slope of Mount Hermon he had collected the plant
that Körnicke had searched for the plant for many years
that the importance of the plant was not recognized when it was collected
that wild emmer grows only on the slopes of Mount Hermon
explanation: Kotschy did not identify the plant, and it waited in the herbarium until Körnicke examined it. (1) contradicts the fact that the place is known, and (2) and (4) are not stated.

steps.stem: According to the third paragraph, which of the following is correct?
choices: Aaronsohn found wild emmer at the place where Kotschy had collected his specimen before he found it anywhere else
Aaronsohn began to search for wild emmer after Schweinfurth told him about Körnicke's identification
Aaronsohn was the first to identify wild emmer as a wild form of cultivated wheat
Aaronsohn found wild emmer only in the area of Rosh Pinna
explanation: Schweinfurth told him of the identification and urged him to search. (1) contradicts the first find near Rosh Pinna, (3) was Körnicke's identification, and (4) contradicts "many other places."

steps.stem: According to the text, Aaronsohn hoped that wild emmer -
choices: would help to breed wheat varieties better suited to dry regions
would replace cultivated wheat in the fields of the region
would prove that wheat had first been cultivated in the Galilee
would be grown at Atlit and sold to farmers in the United States
explanation: He hoped that crossing it with cultivated wheat would produce varieties suited to dry regions. (2), (3) and (4) are not stated.

steps.stem: Which of the following is not implied in the last two paragraphs?
choices: Genes from wild emmer have been used to improve cultivated wheat
Some of the wild emmer used in research came from the area where Aaronsohn made his first find
Knowing the genome of a wild plant can shorten the search for useful genes
After Aaronsohn's death, the station at Atlit was reopened in order to continue his work
explanation: The text says only that his plans were not carried out; nothing is said about reopening the station. (1), (2) and (3) are stated or implied.

steps.stem: The second paragraph describes ____, and the third paragraph describes ____.
choices: the finding of the plant in the field / its identification in a herbarium
the identification of a stored specimen as wild emmer / the finding of the plant growing in the field
the first attempts to grow wild emmer / the reasons for their failure
a disagreement between two botanists about the plant / Aaronsohn's attempt to decide between them by finding it in the field
explanation: Paragraph 2 tells of Körnicke's identification of the specimen, and paragraph 3 of Aaronsohn's finds in the field. (1) reverses the two, and (3) and (4) are not described.

steps.stem: Which of the following is true for both Körnicke and Aaronsohn, according to the text?
choices: Neither of them collected the first known specimen of wild emmer
Each of them saw wild emmer growing in its natural habitat
Each of them was urged by Schweinfurth to search for the plant
Neither of them published his findings about wild emmer during his lifetime
explanation: Kotschy collected the first specimen. (2) and (3) are true only for Aaronsohn, and (4) is not stated for either.

steps.stem: Which of the following is not mentioned in the first paragraph as a reason for draining the swamps of the Hula?
choices: obtaining land that could be cultivated after the water had been removed
creating a reservoir of water for the cities of the coastal plain
reducing the spread of malaria
obtaining land for new settlements
explanation: Land for agriculture and settlements and the fight against malaria are mentioned; a reservoir is not.

steps.stem: According to the second paragraph, which of the following was a consequence of the draining that its planners had not foreseen?
choices: the increase in the area of land available for agriculture
the decrease in the number of mosquitoes in the valley
the declaration of part of the swamp as a nature reserve
the sinking of the ground and the underground fires in the peat
explanation: The unforeseen consequences listed are those of the drying peat. (1) and (2) were the aims of the project, and (3) is described in the third paragraph as a response of nature lovers.

steps.stem: Which of the following best reflects the chain of events described in the second paragraph that affected Lake Kinneret?
choices: the swamps are drained → the Jordan River carries more water → the level of the Kinneret rises → the water in it becomes less salty
the swamps are drained → fish from the Hula move to the Kinneret → the fish population of the Kinneret changes → the quality of its water declines
the peat dries and decomposes → nitrogen compounds are released → rain and irrigation water wash them into the Jordan → they reach the Kinneret
the peat dries and burns → smoke and dust spread over the valley → rain carries the dust into the Kinneret → its water becomes darker
explanation: The paragraph traces the nitrogen compounds from the decomposing peat to the Kinneret. (4) combines the fires and dust, which are mentioned, with a result that is not mentioned; (1) and (2) are not described.

steps.stem: The Hula painted frog (paragraph 3) is mentioned as an example of -
choices: a species that was thought to have disappeared as a result of the draining, but was later found again
a species that returned to the valley after Lake Agmon was created
a species that was described by scientists for the first time after the draining
a species whose disappearance led nature lovers to demand that part of the swamp be kept as the first nature reserve in Israel
explanation: It was declared extinct in 1996 and found again in 2011. (2) links it to Agmon, whereas it was found in the reserve; (3) contradicts 1943; (4) reverses the order, since the reserve was established in 1964, before the frog was declared extinct.

steps.stem: Which of the following statements is not incorrect according to the last paragraph?
choices: Before Lake Agmon was created, cranes did not pass over the Hula Valley
Lake Agmon was created by flooding again the whole area that had been drained in the 1950s
Most of the cranes that pass over the valley in the autumn now remain there for the whole winter, because of the corn
The cranes that stay in the valley in winter are fed in order to reduce the damage they cause to the crops
explanation: The feeding is meant to reduce the damage to the fields. (1) contradicts the fact that the valley is on the migration route, (2) contradicts "part of the drained area," and (3) contradicts the numbers: tens of thousands stay out of hundreds of thousands that pass.

steps.stem: What is the purpose of the last paragraph?
choices: to show that the draining of the Hula was a mistake from the beginning, and that it should not have been carried out
to describe the plans to return Lake Hula to its original size
to show that the partial restoration of the wetland also had consequences that were not planned
to explain why the cranes chose to spend the winter in the Hula Valley
explanation: The paragraph describes the creation of Lake Agmon and the unintended arrival of the cranes. (4) is one detail, (2) contradicts "a small, shallow lake," and (1) is not the paragraph's point.

steps.stem: According to the first paragraph, which of the following is correct?
choices: Most of the buildings that were recognized by UNESCO were built within a period of about thirty years
UNESCO recognized the White City because each of its buildings is an outstanding example of modern architecture
The buildings of the White City were built immediately after Tel Aviv was founded
About four thousand buildings in the International Style were built in Tel Aviv after it was declared a World Heritage Site
explanation: Most were built between the early 1930s and the 1950s. (2) contradicts "not in any single building," (4) reverses the order, and (3) is not stated.

steps.stem: According to the second paragraph, Geddes's plan determined -
choices: the style in which the buildings in the northern part of the city would be built
the location of the buildings that would be designed by architects trained at the Bauhaus
the network of streets and the location of public gardens
the number of floors that could be built on each plot
explanation: The plan set the streets and gardens. (1) contradicts "Geddes did not determine the style of the buildings," and (2) and (4) are not stated.

steps.stem: Which of the following is not presented in the third paragraph as an adaptation of the International Style to the climate of Tel Aviv?
choices: small windows set deep in the walls
long balconies shaded by the balconies of the floor above
raising buildings on columns so that the breeze could pass under them
flat roofs without decoration
explanation: Flat roofs and the absence of decoration are presented as principles the architects brought from Europe, not as changes made because of the climate.

steps.stem: According to the fourth paragraph, the name "White City" -
choices: was given to the area by the founders of Tel Aviv
became widely used several decades after most of the buildings had been built
reflects the fact that all the buildings were plastered in white
was given to the area by UNESCO when it was declared a World Heritage Site
explanation: It became common only after the 1984 exhibition. (3) is contradicted by the light yellow, gray and pink plaster, and (4) contradicts the dates.

steps.stem: According to the last paragraph, allowing owners to build an additional floor on the roof -
choices: is meant to help finance the restoration of the buildings, but may change their appearance
was forbidden by UNESCO when it declared the White City a World Heritage Site
is allowed only for buildings that are not included in the conservation plan
is meant mainly to increase the number of apartments and residents in the center of the city
explanation: The income finances the restoration, and critics say the floors change the buildings' appearance. (3) contradicts the fact that the plan itself allows it, and (2) and (4) are not stated.

steps.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the text?
choices: Geddes designed some of the buildings of the White City
UNESCO required Tel Aviv to remove the additional floors that had been built on the roofs of the buildings
Most of the architects of the White City had studied at the Bauhaus
Some changes made by residents canceled features planned because of the climate
explanation: Residents closed balconies, which had been designed to give shade. (3) contradicts "most had been trained in other schools," (1) contradicts the second paragraph, and (2) is not stated.

steps.stem: According to the first paragraph, which of the following statements about the discovery of the map is not correct?
choices: It was discovered during the construction of a church
Part of it was damaged by the builders of the new church before its importance became known to scholars
It was discovered in the nineteenth century
It was discovered in the course of an excavation whose purpose was to find ancient maps
explanation: The map was uncovered by builders of a new church, not in an excavation aimed at finding maps. (1), (2) and (3) are stated.

steps.stem: "This orientation" (paragraph 2) refers to the fact that -
choices: east is at the top of the map
Jerusalem appears larger than the other places on the map
the names of the places are written in Greek
the map shows the region from Lebanon to the Nile Delta
explanation: The previous sentence says the map is oriented with east at the top. (2) is described only in the third and last paragraphs, and (3) and (4) are not about orientation.

steps.stem: The appearance of the Nea Church on the map is used to determine -
choices: the exact year in which the map was made
the earliest date at which the map could have been made
the latest date at which the map could have been made
the location of the main street of Jerusalem
explanation: The map could not have been made before 543. (1) overstates what the church shows, and (3) reverses the logic.

steps.stem: According to the fourth paragraph, the excavations in the Jewish Quarter -
choices: proved that the map had been made in Jerusalem
showed that the main street shown on the map had not existed in the sixth century
uncovered remains whose locations matched the locations of buildings shown on the map
made it possible to date the map to the year 543
explanation: The locations of the street and the church matched the map. (2) contradicts this, (4) confuses the date of the church with that of the map, and (1) is not stated.

steps.stem: According to the last paragraph, which of the following is the most similar to the way in which places are shown on the map?
choices: an aerial photograph of a city
a map for tourists on which the main sights are drawn much larger than their actual size
an architect's plan of a building, drawn to scale, in which every room is shown in its exact size and position
a list of the streets of a city arranged in alphabetical order
explanation: Important places are shown larger than their size and distances are not accurate. (1) and (3) are exact representations, and (4) shows no space at all.

steps.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the text about the use of the Madaba Map as a historical source?
choices: It is reliable only for the period before the Nea Church was built
It cannot be used as a source at all, since its sizes and distances are not accurate
Its details should be compared with other evidence, such as the findings of excavations
It is the only source for the plan of Jerusalem in the sixth century, and therefore its details cannot be checked
explanation: The last paragraph says each detail should be examined against other evidence, and the excavations are an example. (2) goes too far, since the map matched the excavations; (1) and (4) are not stated.

vop-01.title: Passage 1
paragraphs: Biologists have long observed that island animals often differ in size from their closest relatives on the mainland, and in a predictable direction: species that are large on the mainland tend to become smaller on islands, while species that are small tend to become larger. The fossil record offers striking cases of the first kind. Several Mediterranean islands, Sicily and Malta among them, were once home to dwarf elephants, some of which stood barely a meter high at the shoulder. A living case of the second kind is a rat on the Indonesian island of Flores that weighs several times as much as the common rat. The pattern was first described in 1964 by the zoologist J. Bristol Foster, and it is known today as "the island rule." The pattern, however, is a tendency rather than a law: a great many island species do not differ in size from their mainland relatives at all, and a few have changed in the direction opposite to the one that the pattern predicts.

The most widely accepted explanation concerns food. An island offers a limited supply of food, and its animals cannot move elsewhere when that supply runs short. A large body requires a great deal of food, whereas a smaller individual of the same species can get through a lean season on what remains. Over many generations, therefore, smaller individuals are more likely to survive and leave offspring, and the population as a whole becomes smaller. Some researchers have refined this explanation. According to them, what matters is not the area of the island but the amount of food it provides for each animal: a large island consisting mostly of bare rock may favor small bodies more strongly than a small island covered with dense vegetation.

A second explanation looks not to food but to enemies. Remote islands often have few large predators or none, since such predators need extensive hunting grounds and seldom cross the sea. On the mainland, being small helps an animal to escape by hiding in cracks and burrows, while being very large protects a grazing animal, since few predators can overcome it. Where there are no predators, both advantages lose their value, and body size is free to shift toward whatever suits local conditions best. This explanation accounts for both directions of change by a single cause, whereas the explanation from food is more convincing for the shrinking of large animals than for the growth of small ones. On the other hand, it predicts a change in size on every island that lacks predators, although many such islands are home to species whose size has not changed.

A team of biologists compared the two explanations on a chain of small islands inhabited by a single species of lizard. A predatory snake lives on some of the islands but not on others, and the islands also differ in their vegetation, and hence in the number of insects on which the lizards feed. The researchers reasoned that if the explanation from predators were correct, the lizards on the snake-free islands should differ in size from those on the other islands even where the supply of insects was similar. In fact, the lizards' size corresponded closely to the supply of insects, whereas the presence of snakes made almost no difference. The researchers concluded that on these islands, at least, food is the decisive factor. They added a caution, however: since the snakes reached the islands relatively recently, the lizards may not yet have had time to respond to them.

Neither explanation, then, turns the island pattern into a law. What the island cases do show is something more general: the size of an animal, which we tend to regard as a fixed feature of its species, is in fact a compromise among competing pressures, such as the need for food, the danger from predators and the demands of the climate. When life on an island shifts the balance among these pressures, size shifts with it, and the fossil record suggests that on some islands this happened within a few thousand years.

vop-02.title: Passage 2
paragraphs: According to an ancient Jewish custom, writings that contain the name of God may not be destroyed, even when they are worn out and no longer in use. Such writings were therefore placed in a special storeroom, called a geniza, and from time to time they were taken out and buried. In the Ben Ezra Synagogue in Fustat, the old part of Cairo, this last stage was hardly ever carried out. For hundreds of years, from about the tenth century onward, the members of the community placed in the synagogue's geniza not only worn-out books but almost every piece of paper on which Hebrew letters had been written, and the room was not emptied. The dry climate of Egypt did the rest: when the contents of the room reached the hands of scholars at the end of the nineteenth century, many of the documents were still legible.

Fragments from the Cairo Geniza began to reach dealers and collectors in Europe as early as the 1860s, but their importance was not recognized at once. The turning point came in May 1896, when the twin sisters Agnes Lewis and Margaret Gibson, scholars from Cambridge who had bought a number of fragments in Cairo, showed them to Solomon Schechter, who taught rabbinic literature at the university. Schechter identified one of the fragments as a page from the Hebrew original of the Book of Ben Sira, a work written in the second century BCE, which until then had been known mainly from its Greek translation.

In December of that year Schechter traveled to Cairo, with the support of Charles Taylor, the head of one of the Cambridge colleges, and with a letter of recommendation from the Chief Rabbi of Britain. With the consent of the community's leaders, he removed from the geniza a very large part of its contents, and sent it to Cambridge. The Taylor-Schechter collection, as it is called today, contains close to two hundred thousand fragments. Other parts of the geniza, which had been sold before Schechter's arrival or were removed from the room later, are kept today in dozens of libraries in Europe, the United States and Israel.

The first researchers of the geniza searched mainly for literary and religious works: lost books, early versions of prayers, and liturgical poems that had not been preserved elsewhere. The documentary material - letters, contracts, court records, accounts and lists - received much less attention, although it makes up a considerable part of the collection. Most of these documents were written in Judeo-Arabic, that is, in Arabic written in Hebrew letters. The historian Shelomo Dov Goitein, who taught at the Hebrew University and later at the University of Pennsylvania, devoted decades to these documents. In the six volumes of his work "A Mediterranean Society," which appeared between 1967 and 1993, he used them to describe the daily life of the Jews of the Mediterranean region between the eleventh and the thirteenth centuries: their trade, which reached as far as India, their families, their clothes and their food.

Since most of the geniza documents reached the libraries as torn fragments, one document may be divided among several collections, and a researcher who holds one part of it does not always know where the other parts are. For many years, joining such parts required a scholar who remembered the handwriting of hundreds of documents, or long journeys between libraries. In recent decades, most of the fragments have been photographed and made available on the internet, and computer programs that compare the handwriting and the shape of the pages help researchers to locate parts of the same document.

vop-03.title: Passage 3
paragraphs: In the highlands of the Negev, where on average only about one hundred millimeters of rain fall each year, lie the remains of several ancient towns, among them Avdat, Shivta and Nitzana. The towns were founded by the Nabateans, a people who controlled the trade routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean coast. In 106 CE the Nabatean kingdom was annexed to the Roman Empire, but the towns continued to exist, and some of them reached their peak only in the Byzantine period, in the fifth and sixth centuries. Avdat lay on the road that led from Petra to Gaza. Around them, in the dry beds of the wadis, the remains of thousands of ancient fields can be seen. Such an amount of rain is not enough for growing crops without irrigation, and there are no rivers or springs in the area that could have supplied water to the fields.

The solution to this puzzle lies in the way in which the ancient farmers used the rain. The soil of the area, loess, forms a thin crust on its surface after the first drops of rain, and as a result most of the water that falls on the slopes does not sink into the ground but flows down them. The farmers built low stone walls across the beds of the wadis, and turned them into a series of level terraces. They also dug channels along the slopes, which collected the water that flowed down them and led it to the terraces, where it was held behind the walls and soaked into the soil. Thus each field received not only the rain that fell on it but also the rain that had fallen on an area many times larger. In the systems that have been studied, this ratio was usually about twenty to one, and in some cases as much as thirty to one, so that a field in the wadi received, in practice, several times more water than the rain that fell on it.

In 1959 the botanist Michael Evenari of the Hebrew University, together with the hydrologist Leslie Shanan and the agronomist Naphtali Tadmor, rebuilt one of the ancient farms near Avdat, repairing its walls and channels according to the remains that had been found on the site. In the following years they grew there wheat, barley, vegetables and fruit trees, without any water other than the runoff from the slopes, and in most years the crops were successful. Evenari and his colleagues later described their work in the book "The Negev: The Challenge of a Desert," which was first published in 1971.

The research of Evenari and his colleagues also dealt with a phenomenon that had puzzled earlier visitors: on the slopes above many of the fields there are thousands of small heaps of stones, arranged in rows. The local Arabs called them "grape mounds," and it was commonly believed that vines had been grown on them. Evenari proposed a different explanation. According to him, the heaps were formed when the farmers cleared the stones from the surface of the slopes, since a slope that has been cleared of stones forms a crust more easily, and therefore more water flows down it into the channels.

Although these fields are often called "Nabatean farms," later research has shown that many of them were built or expanded in the Byzantine period, several hundred years after the end of the Nabatean kingdom. Remains of pottery and of buildings near the fields, as well as dates obtained by laboratory methods, have helped researchers to establish when the fields were in use.

vop-04.title: Passage 4
paragraphs: In the winter of 1985-1986, after several years of drought, the level of the Sea of Galilee fell considerably, and wide areas of its shore, which had been covered by water for many years, were exposed. The lake had reached one of its lowest levels in many years. In January 1986, two brothers from Kibbutz Ginosar, Moshe and Yuval Lufan, who were interested in archaeology and used to search the exposed shore for ancient objects, noticed the outline of a wooden boat in the mud, not far from the kibbutz. The antiquities authorities were informed, and an examination of the boat showed that it was very old.

The excavation of the boat, led by the archaeologist Shelley Wachsmann, had to be carried out under difficult conditions. The winter rains had begun, and the level of the lake was expected to rise and cover the site again. The team therefore worked day and night, and completed the excavation in eleven days. Volunteers from the kibbutz and from other places in the area took part in the work. Throughout the work the wood was kept wet, since wood that has been in water for a long time becomes soft, and if it dries quickly it shrinks and cracks. After the excavation, the boat was covered with polyurethane foam, which hardened around it and held it together, and in this form it was floated across the lake to the place where it was to be treated.

The boat is 8.2 meters long and 2.3 meters wide. Its builders used the method that was common in the Mediterranean in that period: the planks were joined to each other by tenons fitted into slots cut in their edges, and only afterwards were the frames added. The planks were made mainly of cedar, and the frames mainly of oak. Researchers who examined the wood identified about twelve different types of wood, some of them of poor quality. The boat had evidently been repaired many times during its long use, and parts of it had been taken from other boats. In its last years, apparently, its useful parts were removed, and what remained was abandoned in the water.

The boat was dated in two ways. A cooking pot and an oil lamp found near it are of types that were common from the first century BCE to the first century CE. The wood itself was dated by carbon-14, and the results pointed to approximately the same period. The boat could have carried about fifteen people, and it was probably used for fishing and for transporting people and goods on the lake. It could be rowed, and it could also be sailed. Since boats of this kind are mentioned in the writings of that period but no boat of that period had been found in the lake before, the discovery aroused great interest, and in the press the boat was even linked to events described in the New Testament.

The conservation of the boat took many years. It was placed in a special pool, and the water in the pool was gradually replaced by a heated solution of polyethylene glycol, a synthetic wax that penetrates the wood and takes the place of the water in its cells. Only when the wood had absorbed enough of the wax could the boat be taken out of the pool without the risk of its collapsing. Throughout this period the temperature and the concentration of the solution were raised gradually, under constant supervision. Since 2000 it has been displayed in a museum at Kibbutz Ginosar.

vop-05.title: Passage 5
paragraphs: In the 1930s, the surface of the Dead Sea was about 390 meters below sea level. Since the 1960s its level has been falling, at first by a few tens of centimeters a year, and since the 1990s by about a meter a year, and by 2016 it had reached about 430 meters below sea level. The shoreline has moved away from the places where it was a few decades ago, and in some places the distance between the old shoreline and the water is now more than a kilometer.

The main reason for the decline is that much less water reaches the lake than in the past. Most of the water that once flowed into it came from the Jordan River and its tributaries. Since the 1960s, Israel, Jordan and Syria have diverted most of this water for drinking and agriculture: Israel through the National Water Carrier, which began to operate in 1964, Jordan through a canal that takes water from the Yarmouk River, and Syria through dams built on the tributaries of the Yarmouk. To this should be added the activity of the mineral industries on both sides of the lake, which pump water from the northern basin into evaporation ponds in the south, in order to extract potash and other minerals from it. In addition, much of the water that still flows in the lower Jordan is sewage and salty water. Since the evaporation from the lake has not decreased, its level falls from year to year.

In the southern part of the lake the situation is different. This shallow basin dried up in the 1970s, and today it consists of evaporation ponds, into which water is pumped from the north. As the water evaporates, salt settles on the floor of the ponds, in a layer that grows thicker by about twenty centimeters every year. As a result, the water level in the ponds is rising, and it threatens the hotels built on their shore at Ein Bokek. Therefore, in this part of the lake, the problem is not the retreat of the water but its rise.

Along the shores of the northern basin a different phenomenon appeared: sinkholes, pits that open suddenly in the ground, some of them several meters deep. The first sinkholes were noticed in the 1980s, and since then their number has grown to several thousand. According to the explanation accepted by researchers at the Geological Survey of Israel, a layer of salt lies buried a few tens of meters under the old shore, a remnant of an earlier lake that existed in the area. As long as the level of the Dead Sea was high, the groundwater in contact with this layer was salty, and could not dissolve it. When the level of the lake fell, the boundary between the salty water and the fresh groundwater that flows from the mountains moved toward the lake, and fresh water reached the salt layer and began to dissolve it. In this way cavities formed under the ground, and when the layer of soil above a cavity could no longer support its own weight, it collapsed.

The sinkholes have caused considerable damage. Parts of roads and of date plantations have had to be abandoned, and bathing beaches on the shore of the lake have been closed. The danger is not only to property. In the early 2000s the geologist Eli Raz of Kibbutz Ein Gedi, who had been documenting the sinkholes for years, fell into a sinkhole that opened under his feet, and was rescued only after many hours.

vop-06.title: Passage 6
paragraphs: The cultivated wheat that feeds a large part of humanity did not develop by itself. Cultivated wheat differs from wild wheat mainly in that its ears do not shatter when the grain ripens, so that the farmer can harvest the grain before it falls to the ground. It is the result of thousands of years of selection by farmers, which began, according to the accepted view, in the region of the Fertile Crescent about ten thousand years ago. For a long time, however, it was not known from which wild plant the first farmers had begun.

The first clue was found in a herbarium. In 1855 the Austrian botanist Theodor Kotschy collected, on the slopes of Mount Hermon, a plant that he did not identify, and a specimen of it was kept in the herbarium in Vienna. Eighteen years later, in 1873, the German botanist Friedrich Körnicke examined the specimen and identified it as a wild form of emmer, one of the most ancient types of cultivated wheat. Emmer was grown in the Middle East and in Egypt for thousands of years, and durum wheat, which is used today to make pasta, developed from it. Körnicke's identification, however, attracted little attention, and no one returned to the area to look for the plant.

The search was renewed at the beginning of the twentieth century by Aaron Aaronsohn, an agronomist who had grown up in Zikhron Ya'akov. The German botanist Georg Schweinfurth told him about Körnicke's identification and urged him to look for the plant, and in 1906 Aaronsohn found wild emmer growing near Rosh Pinna, in the Galilee. In the following years he found it in many other places, including the slopes of Mount Hermon. In 1910 he described his findings in a report published by the United States Department of Agriculture. Aaronsohn did not see in his discovery only an answer to a historical question. The wild plant grew on rocky slopes, in poor soil and with little rain, and he hoped that crossing it with cultivated wheat would make it possible to breed varieties better suited to dry regions. With funds that he raised in the United States, he established in 1910 an agricultural experiment station at Atlit, where he began to collect and study plants of the region.

Aaronsohn's plans were not carried out. The station was damaged during the First World War, and Aaronsohn himself was killed in a plane crash in 1919. Wild emmer, however, continued to interest researchers. In the second half of the twentieth century, Israeli researchers collected hundreds of samples of it in the Galilee and on the Golan Heights, and found that its populations are very diverse. From one of these samples, collected near Rosh Pinna, a gene was identified that gives resistance to stripe rust, a fungal disease that damages wheat, and it has been introduced into cultivated varieties. This gene, known as Yr15, is today used by wheat breeders in many countries. Another gene taken from wild emmer increases the protein content of the grain.

In 2017, an international team led by researchers from Tel Aviv University published the full sequence of the genome of wild emmer. The genome of wild emmer is very large - several times larger than the human genome - and for many years this made its sequencing difficult. The researchers pointed out that knowing the genome makes it much easier to locate genes that could be useful for improving cultivated wheat, a task that in the past required years of crossing and selection.

vop-07.title: Passage 7
paragraphs: Until the 1950s, a considerable part of the Hula Valley, in the north of the country, was covered by a shallow lake, Lake Hula, and by extensive swamps of papyrus and reeds that surrounded it. For the Jewish settlers who came to the valley at the beginning of the twentieth century, the swamps were an obstacle: the land they covered could not be cultivated, and the mosquitoes that bred in them spread malaria. The idea of draining them was raised as early as the 1930s, and between 1951 and 1958 it was carried out by the Jewish National Fund. The channel of the Jordan River south of the lake was deepened, the rock threshold that had held the water back was lowered, and new canals were dug to carry the water out of the valley. The lake and most of the swamps disappeared, and tens of thousands of dunams of new land were made available for agriculture and for new settlements.

At first, the project was regarded as one of the great achievements of the young state. Within two decades, however, it became clear that it had consequences that its planners had not foreseen. The soil that had been exposed was peat, which is made of plant remains that had accumulated for thousands of years under water. When it dried, it began to decompose. In some places the ground sank by more than a meter, fires broke out under the surface and burned for months, and the wind lifted clouds of dust from the fields. The decomposition of the peat also released large amounts of nitrogen compounds, which rain and irrigation water washed into the Jordan, and from there into Lake Kinneret, the country's main source of drinking water, where they harmed the quality of the water.

The draining also harmed the plants and animals of the valley. Several species of fish and plants that had lived in the lake and in the swamps disappeared from the area, and the Hula painted frog, which had been described by scientists only in 1943, was not seen again after 1955, and in 1996 it was declared extinct. Already during the draining, nature lovers had demanded that part of the swamp be kept, and in 1964 a small area was declared a nature reserve, the first in Israel. In 2011 a Hula painted frog was found in the reserve, and since then more have been found.

In the 1990s, in an attempt to solve the problems of the peat, part of the drained area was flooded again, and a small, shallow lake, called Lake Agmon, was created. Raising the level of the groundwater slowed the decomposition of the peat and the sinking of the ground, but the new lake also brought a result that its planners had not intended. The Hula Valley lies on one of the main routes of bird migration between Europe and Africa, and every autumn hundreds of thousands of cranes pass over it. After the lake was created, the number of cranes that stayed in the valley for the whole winter grew from a few hundred to tens of thousands, and the birds began to feed in the farmers' fields and to cause heavy damage to the crops. The solution that was found was to feed the cranes: every day, several tons of corn are spread in a certain area near the lake, and the cranes, which find enough food there, cause less damage to the fields. The cranes have become a tourist attraction, and today tens of thousands of people come to the valley every winter to watch them.

vop-08.title: Passage 8
paragraphs: In 2003 UNESCO declared the "White City" of Tel Aviv a World Heritage Site. The declaration refers to about four thousand buildings in the International Style, most of which were built between the early 1930s and the 1950s, in the center of the city. According to UNESCO, the importance of these buildings lies not in any single building but in the fact that so many of them, built within a short period, have been preserved together, and in the way in which the principles of modern European architecture were adapted to local conditions.

The streets on which these buildings stand had been planned before most of them were built. In 1925 the Scottish town planner Patrick Geddes prepared a plan for the northern part of Tel Aviv, which was then still mostly sand dunes. The plan determined a network of main streets running parallel to the sea and quieter residential streets between them, and set aside land for public gardens in the center of the blocks. Geddes, who had also worked in India, believed that a city should be planned as a whole, and not street by street. Geddes did not determine the style of the buildings, and the first buildings built according to his plan were in a variety of styles.

In the 1930s, many architects who had studied in Europe arrived in the country, some of them after the Nazis came to power in Germany. A few of them, such as Arieh Sharon and Shmuel Mestechkin, had studied at the Bauhaus, the German school of design and architecture, but most had been trained in other schools. They brought with them the principles of the International Style: simple geometric forms, flat roofs and the absence of decoration. The climate of Tel Aviv, however, is very different from that of Europe, and the architects changed the style accordingly. Instead of the large windows common in Europe, they used smaller windows, set deep in the walls, which let in less sunlight. They built long balconies, which were shaded by the balconies of the floor above, and raised many of the buildings on columns, so that the sea breeze could pass under them. The narrow horizontal windows that lit the stairwells became one of the characteristic features of these buildings. Other typical features were rounded corners and long horizontal bands of windows and balconies.

The name "White City" became common only several decades later. It was given wide publicity in 1984, in an exhibition on the International Style in Israel, curated by the architect Michael Levin at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art. The exhibition presented the buildings of the 1930s as a unique architectural heritage, and contributed to the public demand to preserve them. In fact, not all the buildings were white: many were plastered in light shades of yellow, gray or pink.

Over the years, many of the buildings deteriorated. The salty sea air damaged the plaster and the iron, and many residents closed their balconies with walls or shutters in order to add a room to their apartments. In 2008 the city approved a conservation plan, which includes about a thousand buildings. To encourage the owners to restore them, the plan allows, in many cases, an additional floor to be built on the roof, and the income from it helps to finance the restoration. Some of the buildings have already been restored, and in others the restoration has not yet begun. Critics of the plan argue that the additional floors change the appearance of the buildings that the plan is meant to preserve.

vop-09.title: Passage 9
paragraphs: In 1884, while a new church was being built in the town of Madaba, east of the Jordan River, the builders uncovered the mosaic floor of an ancient church that had stood on the same site. Part of the floor was damaged during the construction work, and only in 1896 did its importance become known to scholars. The mosaic turned out to be a map of the Land of Israel and the neighboring regions, from Lebanon in the north to the Nile Delta in the south, made in the sixth century. It is the oldest map of the region that has survived in its original form. Madaba was then a town with many churches decorated with mosaics, and many of them have been uncovered since.

Only part of the original map has survived, but even this part contains the names of about one hundred and fifty places, written in Greek, together with pictures of towns, rivers and mountains. Among the places shown are Jericho, surrounded by palm trees, and Gaza, Ashkelon and other towns on the coast. Like many ancient maps, it is oriented with east at the top, so that the Mediterranean Sea appears at the bottom and the desert at the top. This orientation, which may seem strange to a modern observer, corresponded to the direction in which the church faced, so that each place on the map lay in the same direction as the real place. The Dead Sea appears with two boats on it, and in the Jordan River there are fish, some of which are shown turning back, as if to avoid its salty water.

The largest and most detailed picture on the map is that of Jerusalem. The city is surrounded by a wall with towers, and it is crossed by a main street lined with columns, which leads from the gate in the north to the south of the city. Along the street, several churches can be identified. One of them is the "New Church" of Mary, known as the Nea, which the emperor Justinian dedicated in 543. The appearance of this church on the map indicates that the map could not have been made before it was built, and most scholars therefore date the map to the second half of the sixth century.

For many years, scholars could compare the picture of Jerusalem on the map only with the written sources. After 1967, excavations in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City, directed by the archaeologist Nahman Avigad, uncovered the remains of a street lined with columns in the southern part of the city, as well as the remains of a very large church, which were identified as the remains of the Nea. The locations of these remains matched their locations on the map. Some of the columns of the street were set up again in their places, and today they can be seen by visitors to the Jewish Quarter.

Nevertheless, scholars warn against treating the map as a precise plan. Its makers did not draw it to scale: important places, and Jerusalem above all, are shown much larger than their actual size, and the distances between places are not accurate. The map was made for worshippers, who saw in it mainly the holy places, and it presents what its makers considered important. Therefore, each of its details should be examined against other evidence before conclusions are drawn from it. In addition, the mosaic itself has been damaged more than once since its discovery, and parts of it were restored in the twentieth century.
